title: Shop Bill
description: Price many things from one price tag, share money equally, fill a bill and find its total, and count a purse against a price.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Find the cost of many things by multiplying the price of one, share money equally by dividing, write a bill with the cost of each line and the total, and say whether the money in a purse is enough and by how much.
writeup.look: A shop counter with a shelf and an amber price tag, a sky blue count box, a tray of money and a row of plates, a bill table with a green total, a purse and a price tag on a balance, a words card under them, the Times, Share, Bill and Purse buttons, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Shop Bill' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many things have been priced. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A plain shop counter fills the working area. The shelf stands at x 110, y 230, 560 by 230, and holds a row of at most nine of one kind of thing, each drawn large enough to count, such as pencil boxes, with an amber price tag hanging at its left end that reads the price of one. The sky blue count box sits at x 110, y 480, 190 by 70, with a plus and a minus, and a sky blue bracket under the row reads how many. The Times button stands at x 330, y 480, 150 by 70 and lays one copy of the price tag under every thing. The tray of money stands at x 700, y 230, 330 by 110, above a row of at most six plates at x 700, y 360, each drawn large enough to hold a small pile of flat notes and discs, with the Plates box at x 700, y 480, 190 by 70. In the Bill view the bill replaces the shelf, at x 110, y 216, 960 by 300: a table of four columns headed Thing, How many, Price of one and Cost, at most three lines, a rule under the last line and a green Total below it. In the Purse view the balance stands across the working area with the purse of notes and coins on its left pan at x 160, y 300 and the price tag on its right pan at x 700, y 300, and the gap is lit green when the balance has tipped. The words card stands under the shelf at x 110, y 566, 960 by 90, and says the step in writing, such as the price of one times how many. The Times, Share, Bill and Purse buttons stand in a row at x 110, y 666, each 150 by 60, labelled in words. A green Answer tag at x 700, y 480, 330 by 70, holds what the child has typed. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the cost, the share, the total or the difference into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag and a label. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. A note is a plain flat rectangle in its own colour and a coin a plain round disc, each with its value in large near-black type, so a value is read from the number and never from the colour. Anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because an amount is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The shop shows the last thing worked out, with the words card saying the step aloud and in writing and the green Answer tag beside it.

phases.win: the price tags line up under the things, the cost counts up, and a green Answer tag settles
phases.does: sets how many with the count box, watches the price tag repeat once for each thing, and types the cost
phases.goal: the cost of many is the price of one times how many, and the answer is a number of rupees
phases.says: Look at the price of one. How many will you buy?
phases.check: Away from the screen: one pencil costs Rs 9. Do 4 pencils cost more or less than 1 pencil? Say how you know.
phases.feels: the price of one repeating under every thing as the count goes up, and the cost counting up with it
phases.hands: Set out a few classroom things with a price label on one of them, and have a child put the same label by every thing and then say the cost out loud.
phases.tries: First rung: say the price of one and how many. Second rung: count the price tags laid out under the things. Third rung: the same task with only two things, before more are added.

wrong.why: both numbers are on the shelf and adding is the sum a child knows best
wrong.move: adds the price and the count, so the cost of many comes out near the price of one
wrong.screen: the price tag is laid out once under every thing, each copy lit in turn, and the costs are counted up copy by copy until the child sees the cost grows by the price each time

wrong.why: a big number seems to ask for sharing
wrong.move: divides the price of one by how many because the numbers look big
wrong.screen: the shelf is shown again with the price tags laid out under the things, and the words card says the cost of many is more than the price of one

phases.screen: a shelf holds a row of one kind of thing with an amber price tag and a sky blue count box beside it
phases.soWhat: the cost of many is the price of one times how many, and the answer is a number of rupees

phases.win: every plate holds the same pile, the tray is empty, and a green tag reads what one plate holds
phases.does: sets how many plates, watches the money dealt out one at a time, and types what one plate holds
phases.goal: to share money equally, or to find the cost of one, we divide the money by the number of plates
phases.says: Share the money so that every plate gets the same.
phases.check: Away from the screen: Rs 60 is shared equally by 5 friends. Does each friend get more or less than Rs 60? Why?
phases.feels: the money going out onto the plates one at a time until every plate holds the same pile
phases.hands: Give a child a small bag of play money and some paper plates, and have them deal it out one at a time until every plate holds the same.
phases.tries: First rung: say how many plates there are. Second rung: watch the money dealt out one at a time. Third rung: the same task with two plates only, before more plates are added.

wrong.why: multiplying was the sum of the last phase and it is still in mind
wrong.move: multiplies the money by the plates instead of sharing it out
wrong.screen: the tray is shown again and dealt out onto the plates one note or coin at a time, and the words card says that sharing equally makes the pile on each plate smaller

wrong.why: the plates are the only thing in a row that can be counted
wrong.move: gives the answer as the number of plates
wrong.screen: one plate is lit and its pile counted aloud, and the words card says that the answer is what one plate holds, in rupees

phases.screen: a tray of money stands above a row of empty plates, with a plus and a minus for the plates
phases.soWhat: to share money equally, or to find the cost of one, divide the money by the number of plates

phases.win: each cost drops into its line, the lines slide down to the rule, and the green Total lights
phases.does: fills the cost of each line from its price and its count, then adds the lines and types the total
phases.goal: a bill has a line for each thing, the cost of a line is the price of one times how many, and the total is the lines added
phases.says: Find the cost of each line. Then find the total.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a bill has 2 pens at Rs 7 each and 1 ruler at Rs 12. Say the cost of each line, and then the total.
phases.feels: each cost dropping into its own line and the lines sliding down to the rule to make the total
phases.hands: Draw a bill with three lines on the board. Ask for the cost of each line before anyone writes a total, and add the lines together at the end.
phases.tries: First rung: say the price of one and how many for one line. Second rung: find the cost of that line only. Third rung: the same bill with two lines only, before the third is added.

wrong.why: the price of one is the only amber number in sight
wrong.move: adds the prices of one in a bill and leaves out how many of each
wrong.screen: each line is lit in turn and its cost made by laying the price of one out as many times as the count says, so the cost of the line is seen before any adding

wrong.why: the last line is the one nearest the rule
wrong.move: types the cost of the last line as the total
wrong.screen: the lines slide down to the rule one at a time and the running total is shown after each, so the total is seen to be every line added

phases.screen: a bill on the counter, a table of the thing, how many, the price of one and the cost, with a rule under it
phases.soWhat: a bill has a line for each thing, the cost of a line is the price of one times how many, and the total is the lines added
phases.concept: A bill: the cost of each thing and the total

phases.win: the balance tips to the larger side, the gap lights green, and the words card says how much
phases.does: counts the purse, compares it with the price, says enough or not, and types what is left or still needed
phases.goal: the money in a purse is counted together, then set against the price to see which is more and by how much
phases.says: Count the money in the purse. Is it enough for the price?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a purse holds Rs 65 and a toy costs Rs 70. Is the money enough? What do you say about the Rs 5?
phases.feels: the balance tipping to the larger side and the gap between the purse and the price lighting up
phases.hands: Fill a small bag with dummy notes and coins, count it aloud with a partner, and set a price label next to it to say which is more.
phases.tries: First rung: count the notes and coins one at a time. Second rung: say which is more, the purse or the price. Third rung: the same task with a purse of two things only, before more are added.

wrong.why: the largest note is the first one noticed
wrong.move: compares the biggest note with the price and ignores the rest of the purse
wrong.screen: the whole purse is counted note by note and coin by coin on the pan, and the running amount is shown, so the money is seen to be all of it together

wrong.why: a full purse looks like a lot of money
wrong.move: says enough because the purse looks heavy
wrong.screen: the balance tips only when the two amounts are compared, and the gap is lit and counted in rupees, so the child sees which side is more and by how much

phases.screen: a purse of notes and coins on one pan of a balance and a price tag on the other pan
phases.soWhat: the money in a purse is counted together and set against the price, and the difference is what is left or still needed

writeup.delight: On the first phase, as the count goes up, the price tag is copied once under every new thing and the cost under the row counts up one price at a time. On the fourth phase, when the child has typed the difference, the balance settles level with a soft click as the gap is made up by the missing money, or the extra money lifts out of the purse and rests beside it.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a shelf of one kind of thing stands at the left with an amber price tag on it and a sky blue count box beside it, and the Answer tag is empty. On the second a tray of money stands above a row of empty plates, with a plus and a minus for the plates. On the third a bill lies on the counter with its lines of the thing, how many and the price of one filled in and every cost left empty. On the fourth a purse of notes and coins stands on one pan of a balance and a price tag on the other. One thing moves, once: the price tag gives one slow swing while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on a button is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any price and any count on the shelf, any amount shared out, any bill and any purse against any price, with the words card open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the cost of many, equal shares, a bill with a total and a purse against a price, each at a small shop or stall.
voiceLines: A shelf of things with price tags, and a purse waiting on the counter.
Look at the price of one. How many will you buy?
Share the money so that every plate gets the same.
Find the cost of each line. Then find the total.
Count the money in the purse. Is it enough for the price?
A new shelf. What will you find out first?
Free play. Set any price and any count, and watch what happens.
Look at the price of one again. Ask what the question wants, and try once more.
You worked out every price and every bill by yourself.

observations.why: the cost of many is the price of one taken as many times as there are things.
observations.soWhat: to find the cost of many, multiply the price of one by how many.
observations.observe: As the count went up by one, the price tag was laid out once more and the cost grew by the same step.

observations.why: sharing equally gives every plate the same, so the whole amount is divided by the plates.
observations.soWhat: to share money equally, or to find the cost of one, divide the money by the number.
observations.observe: When the money was dealt out, every plate ended with the same pile and the tray was empty.

observations.why: the cost of a line is the price of one times how many, and the total is every line added.
observations.soWhat: find the cost of each line first, then add the lines for the total.
observations.observe: Each line of the bill got its own cost first, and only then were the costs added into the total.

observations.why: the side with more money weighs more, and the gap between them is the difference.
observations.soWhat: count the purse, compare it with the price, and the difference is what is left or still needed.
observations.observe: The balance tipped to the purse when it held more than the price, and to the price when it held less.

phases.screen: a shelf holds a row of one kind of thing with an amber price tag and a sky blue count box beside it
phases.win: the price tags line up under the things, the cost counts up, and a green Answer tag settles
phases.traceback: The price tags stay under every thing and the running cost is written under each tag in turn, stopping one tag short.
ladder: Add Rs 32 once for every notebook on the counter.
Every eraser has its own tag, so add all the tags.
Nine tags of Rs 26 make the cost of all the pens.
Count the price tags under the things, then add them up.
Many things never cost less than one thing, so multiply the price.

phases.screen: a tray of money stands above a row of empty plates, with a plus and a minus for the plates
phases.win: every plate holds the same pile, the tray is empty, and a green tag reads what one plate holds
phases.traceback: One plate is lit and its notes and coins are added one by one, stopping before the last piece.
ladder: One plate is one friend's share, so add the money on it.
Add up the notes and coins on just one plate.
Each plate is one child's part, so count one plate.
Sharing makes each pile smaller than the whole amount.
Count the money on one plate only and say it in rupees.

phases.screen: a bill on the counter, a table of the thing, how many, the price of one and the cost, with a rule under it
phases.win: each cost drops into its line, the lines slide down to the rule, and the green Total lights
phases.traceback: Each line is lit in turn and the running total is written under the bill, stopping before the last line is added.
ladder: Add the three line totals, not the prices of one.
Add the cost of both lines to get the bill total.
Start with the top line and keep adding each line below it.
Add the first two lines, then add the next one.
The Total column holds the line costs, so add that column.

phases.screen: a purse of notes and coins on one pan of a balance and a price tag on the other pan
phases.win: the balance tips to the larger side, the gap lights green, and the words card says how much
phases.traceback: The purse total and the price are lit and the subtraction is written, the bigger amount first, without its result.
ladder: Take the price away from the money in the purse.
Count on from Rs 74 up to the money in the purse.
The price is more than the purse, so find the gap between them.
Put the two amounts side by side and see which is bigger.
Subtract the smaller amount from the bigger one, in rupees.

items.win: Yes, the bill comes to Rs 157.
Yes, the bill total is Rs 261.
Yes, it is enough and Rs 7 is left.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, no colour means good or bad. The miss empties the answer slot at once (every digit, every box, a picked choice), so it is empty through the traceback; the pad re-opens empty after it.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The price tags stay under every thing and the running cost is written under each tag in turn, stopping one tag short.
Phase 2: One plate is lit and its notes and coins are added one by one, stopping before the last piece.
Phase 3: Each line is lit in turn and the running total is written under the bill, stopping before the last line is added.
Phase 4: The purse total and the price are lit and the subtraction is written, the bigger amount first, without its result.

voice.opening: A shelf of things with price tags, and a purse waiting on the counter.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play: change the price and how many, and watch the cost grow.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: You worked out every price and every bill by yourself.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: A zoo ticket costs Rs 32. What do 5 tickets cost?

question.en: One notebook costs Rs 32, so what do 5 notebooks cost?

items.planQuestion: A sticker sheet costs Rs 8. What do 6 sticker sheets cost?

question.en: What do 6 erasers cost at Rs 8 each?

items.planAnswer: Rs 48, because Rs 8 times 6 is Rs 48 in all

items.planQuestion: A class buys 9 museum tickets at Rs 26 each. What do all the tickets cost?

question.en: A class buys 9 pens at Rs 26 each, so what do they cost in all?

items.planAnswer: Rs 234, because Rs 26 times 9 is Rs 234 in all

items.planQuestion: Rs 216 is shared equally by 6 friends. How much does each friend get?

question.en: Rs 216 is shared equally by 6 friends, so how much does each friend get?

items.planQuestion: Rs 63 is shared equally by 3 friends. How much does each friend get?

question.en: Share Rs 63 equally among 3 friends: how much is one share?

items.planAnswer: Rs 21 each, because Rs 63 divided by 3 is Rs 21 for each friend

items.planQuestion: 8 notebooks cost Rs 192 in all, and every notebook has the same price. What does 1 notebook cost?

question.en: Rs 192 is split equally among 8 children: how much does one child get?

items.planAnswer: Rs 24, because Rs 192 divided by 8 is Rs 24 for each notebook

items.planQuestion: A party shop bill has 3 lines. 4 balloons cost Rs 9 each. 2 caps cost Rs 44 each. 1 mask costs Rs 33. What is the total?

question.en: Tap each empty Total box to fill this bill, then find the bill total.

items.planQuestion: At a fruit stall, oranges cost Rs 11 each and a melon costs Rs 46. A bill has 3 oranges and 1 melon. What is the total?

question.en: Fill in this bill the same way and find what it comes to.

items.planAnswer: Rs 79. Rs 11 times 3 is Rs 33 for the oranges, and Rs 33 plus Rs 46 is Rs 79 in all

items.planQuestion: A snack stall bill has 3 lines. 4 packets of biscuits cost Rs 23 each. 3 juice cartons cost Rs 19 each. 2 bags of nuts cost Rs 56 each. What is the total?

question.en: What does this three-line bill come to in all?

items.planAnswer: Rs 261. Rs 23 times 4 is Rs 92 for the biscuits. Rs 19 times 3 is Rs 57 for the juice. Rs 56 times 2 is Rs 112 for the nuts. Rs 92 plus Rs 57 is Rs 149 so far, and Rs 149 plus Rs 112 is Rs 261 in all

items.planQuestion: A child has 1 note of Rs 200, 2 notes of Rs 20 and 3 coins of Rs 2. A skipping rope costs Rs 239. Is there enough money? How much is left?

question.en: The price is Rs 239: is the purse enough, and how much is left or more needed?

items.planAnswer: Yes. The money is Rs 246 and the rope costs Rs 239, so Rs 7 is left.

items.planQuestion: A purse holds 1 note of Rs 50 and 3 coins of Rs 10. A pen set costs Rs 74. Is there enough money? How much is left or still needed?

question.en: Count the purse against a price of Rs 74: how much is left or more needed?

items.planAnswer: Yes. The purse holds Rs 80, and Rs 80 minus Rs 74 is Rs 6 left over

items.planQuestion: A family has 1 note of Rs 500, 1 note of Rs 200, 2 coins of Rs 20 and 1 coin of Rs 5. They want 4 school bags. Each bag costs Rs 188. Is the money enough? How much more is needed or left?

question.en: The price is 4 bags at Rs 188 each: how much is left or more needed?

items.planAnswer: No. Rs 188 times 4 is Rs 752 in all. The money is Rs 745, and Rs 752 minus Rs 745 is Rs 7 more needed

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.
